evidence: Clear separation into logical layers: context, http, json, model (core/generated), security, util, exception, each with distinct responsibilities
Model layer split into core (domain abstractions, interfaces like BunqModel, AnchorObjectInterface) and generated (API response models), indicating strict layered separation
HTTP layer depends on context and model layers but not vice versa; JSON layer depends on model; context depends on HTTP and security — unidirectional dependencies typical of layered architecture
Fan-out average of 1.98 and max directory depth of 5 suggest controlled internal coupling and layered structure
Tests follow the same layering (e.g., test_context, test_http, test_model), reinforcing the layered organization

Core interfaces (e.g., AnchorObjectInterface) and abstract models (BunqModel) encapsulate domain logic, while adapters (JSON adapters) and clients (HttpClient) isolate external concerns—classic layered pattern with adapters
risks: Generated models and internal models are somewhat tightly coupled (e.g., internal model classes inherit from generated ones), which may reduce flexibility if API contracts evolve
Some services (e.g., ApiContext) coordinate across multiple layers—risk of overloading high-level components if not carefully managed
